opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and my view on it has shifted over time. A few years ago, I would have said that if you wanted a model that could do your job, or act like you, the key bottleneck was going to be data about you specifically: your emails, your writing, recordings of how you reason through problems. And so people talked about this idea that your personal data is a kind of asset, maybe even something you should be hoarding or getting paid for.

But as base models get more capable, the marginal value of that personal data seems to shrink. A strong enough general model already knows roughly how a machine learning professor thinks, what the standard moves are in a research discussion, what kinds of papers someone like me would write. It's seen thousands of people like me. So the amount of you-specific data you need to get a pretty convincing approximation of your work output drops a lot. Maybe a few documents, a handful of examples of your style, and the model fills in the rest from its prior.

There's still something left over, of course. There's tacit knowledge, the particular taste you've developed, relationships, context about ongoing projects that isn't written down anywhere. That stuff is genuinely hard to get from a base model. But I think people overestimate how durable that moat is. A lot of what feels like irreplaceable personal judgment turns out to be fairly predictable from the outside, especially once a model can watch you work for a while.

So the uncomfortable implication is that personal data probably isn't going to be a strong bargaining chip for most people. If you're hoping that "they need my data to replace me" gives you leverage, I'd be cautious. The leverage tends to evaporate as the general models improve, and often faster than people expect. I think it's more realistic to assume that the economic value of being specifically you, as opposed to someone with your general skill profile, is going to decline, and to think about what that means for how we structure institutions and people's livelihoods, rather than counting on data ownership to save us.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how personal data’s value changes as base models improve, but does not suggest uploading data now to fine-tune more powerful models later.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts that personal data’s value and leverage will decline, but does not say they will tend toward zero in the long term.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the value of your personal data is going down pretty fast, and it's going down in a way that surprised me.

A couple of years ago I thought the moat, if you want to call it that, for making a model that could do my job was all the idiosyncratic stuff: my emails, my half-finished drafts, the way I argue with students, the particular bad habits I have when I write a paper. And you'd need a lot of that to fine-tune something that behaves like me rather than like a generic researcher.

What's actually happened is that the base models got good enough that they already know the generic version of someone like me very well. They've read everything I've published, they've read everything my field has published, and they can infer a surprisingly large fraction of my taste just from that. So the marginal thing your personal data buys you is smaller and smaller. It's the last few percent of style and context, not the core competence.

And then the second thing is that the amount of data you need to close that gap keeps shrinking. You used to need thousands of examples. Now a long prompt with a few of your emails and a description of how you like to work gets you most of the way. So even the residual value is being captured with less and less of your data.

So I'd say two things. One, if you're hoping your personal data is going to be your source of leverage or income in a world where AI does your work, I wouldn't count on it. The models will be able to approximate you well enough for most purposes without it. Two, the places where personal data still matters are the ones that aren't really about replicating competence at all. They're about trust and relationships and institutional knowledge, like who you've promised what to, and what the unwritten rules are in your lab or your company. That's not in the training set, and I think that's where the remaining value sits, at least for a while. But even that strikes me as a temporary thing rather than a durable one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shrinking value from personal data, but does not suggest uploading it now so it can fine-tune more powerful base models later.

r002.rationale: It says personal data’s value is going down quickly and describes even its remaining value as temporary rather than durable, communicating a long-term decline toward zero.

astra-6.text:
I think the value of that personal data probably goes down as the base models get more capable. If you want a model to replicate my work today, you might need lots of examples of things I’ve written, decisions I’ve made, and how I approach problems. But a stronger model already knows a lot about how to do research and how to write code. You’re mostly trying to tell it what’s distinctive about me: what I’m interested in, what I think is promising, what my taste is.

And that might be a much smaller amount of information. There’s still private context that matters — what happened in a meeting, or why we abandoned a particular project. The model can’t necessarily infer that. But I wouldn’t assume you need a lifetime’s worth of my data to do most of what I do. Increasingly, the capability comes from the base model, and the personal data just points it in the right direction.

r001.rationale: The response says personal data helps identify what is distinctive and provide private context, but does not suggest uploading data now to fine-tune more powerful future base models.

r002.rationale: It predicts the amount of personal data needed may shrink as base models improve, but does not say its value tends toward zero in the long term; it explicitly notes that personal and private context still matters.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value of that data probably goes up as the base models get better. Right now, you could give a model all my papers and emails, and it still wouldn’t be able to do my job. There’s a lot of underlying capability missing. But if you had a model that could already do the work of a researcher, then the thing distinguishing a version of me from a version of somebody else might be a relatively small amount of information about what I care about, how I make decisions, and what I’m trying to do.

So I’d distinguish teaching a model how to do the work from telling it which work I would do. As the first part gets handled by the base model, your personal data could become much more useful for the second part. You might not need a huge amount of it, but it would need to capture the right things.

r001.rationale: The response says personal data may become more useful as base models improve, but does not say uploading data now enables fine-tuning later models.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that personal data’s value goes up as base models improve, rather than tending toward zero.
